So a constant baseline shift across most rows would still register as high mean absolute SHAP without necessarily being predictive of overfitting. What concerns me more is that this missingness flag is essentially a proxy for loan vintage (old vs new), since missingness rates differ so sharply pre/post ~2015. That means the model may have latched onto vintage-specific default-rate baselines from training years (due to seasoning, macro conditions, censoring) rather than a genuine credit risk signal—a subtle form of temporal leakage.

Since 2017 test data resembles 2016 in "not missing" status, the model gets an easy shortcut for separating the "new vintage" bucket, which could inflate held-out AUC without reflecting real generalizable skill. If a future cohort (2018+) has a different data collection pattern, this shortcut could break down—though for now, the fact that 2016 and 2017 share the same missingness pattern means the immediate next-year test result may still hold up.

Still, I want to check whether these near-constant missingness indicators actually move AUC at all, since AUC depends on rank ordering rather than absolute feature values—if a feature is essentially constant across the test set, it shouldn't meaningfully affect discrimination even if SHAP flags it as important.

But this points to a deeper data availability issue: fields like all_util, open_acc_6m, and related credit-utilization variables only became available from a certain date onward, so the model may have learned patterns skewed by which years had complete versus missing data for these features.

That said, the audit question isn't just whether this modeling choice biases the estimate, but whether it violates the assumption that held-out performance predicts future performance. Since coverage went from full in 2014, near-full in 2015, to zero in 2016 and 2017 alike, the pattern likely persists into 2018+, so this particular field probably isn't misleading.
